nav.def: The fund's total worth right now: cash plus the market value of everything it holds.
nav.example: If GRQ holds $18,000 of stock and $7,000 of cash, its NAV is $25,000.

acb.def: Your average cost per share, commissions included. The CRA uses it to figure your capital gain when you sell.
acb.example: Buy 10 shares at $20 plus a $5 commission and your ACB is $20.50 a share.

day-pnl.def: How much the fund's value moved today — in dollars and percent — versus where it opened this morning.
day-pnl.example: Open at $25,000, sit at $25,300 by lunch, and the day P&L is +$300 (+1.2%).

total-pnl.def: Profit or loss since day one: current NAV minus every dollar ever contributed.
total-pnl.example: Contribute $25,000 over time, sit at a $28,000 NAV, and your total P&L is +$3,000.

vs-xic.def: What your contributions would be worth if you'd just bought XIC, an ETF holding the whole TSX. Beating it is the bar GRQ has to clear to justify existing.
vs-xic.example: If GRQ is up 6% while XIC is up 9%, the fund is losing to the couch-potato option — by 3 points.

drawdown.def: How far NAV has fallen from its highest point. Hit −15% and the kill switch trips automatically.
drawdown.example: NAV peaks at $30,000 then dips to $27,600 — that's an −8% drawdown.

kill-switch.def: A hard stop, enforced in code, that halts all trading instantly. Either member can flip it; nothing trades while it's engaged.
kill-switch.example: Flip it before a volatile earnings print and no order can leave the gate until you flip it back.

cash-floor.def: The minimum share of NAV that must stay in cash, so the fund is never fully committed. Set by the risk dial.
cash-floor.example: A 20% cash floor on a $25,000 fund keeps at least $5,000 in cash — dry powder the gate won't let it spend.

superficial-loss.def: A CRA rule: sell at a loss and rebuy the same name within 30 days and the loss is denied. The agent is barred from tripping it.
superficial-loss.example: Sell XYZ at a loss Monday, rebuy it Friday, and the CRA throws the loss out — you wasted the tax break.

round-trip.def: Commission to buy plus commission to sell. A trade has to be worth at least 3× this to be allowed — fees are the enemy of a small account.
round-trip.example: Two $5 commissions = a $10 round trip, so GRQ won't take the trade unless it expects to clear at least $30.

rsi.def: A 0–100 momentum gauge. Below 30 is 'oversold' (maybe due for a bounce), above 70 'overbought'. An input, not a verdict.
rsi.example: A name selling off to RSI 24 is 'oversold' — stretched low, but cheap-and-falling is still falling.

macd.def: Moving Average Convergence Divergence — tracks whether short-term momentum is pulling ahead of, or falling behind, the longer trend.
macd.example: When MACD crosses above its signal line, short-term momentum just turned up — a bullish nudge, not a verdict.

sma.def: The average closing price over the last N days (SMA50 ≈ 10 weeks). Smooths out daily noise to show the underlying trend.
sma.example: A stock bouncing off its rising 50-day SMA is often read as the uptrend holding.

trend.def: Up- or down-trend read from the moving averages: price above its 50-day average, and the 50-day above the 200-day, is the classic 'uptrend' stack.
trend.example: Price > 50-day > 200-day is the textbook uptrend; flip the order and it's a downtrend.

volatility.def: How much the price swings, annualized from the last ~20 days — a regime gauge (calm / normal / spicy), not a buy/sell signal. It tells you how bumpy the ride is.
volatility.example: A biotech that swings 6% a day is high-volatility — bigger gains, bigger gut-checks — vs a utility that barely moves.

recommendation.def: A confidence-weighted consensus of the directional signals (trend, rsi, macd). The % is the share of signal-confidence behind the call — advisory, not the agent's decision.
recommendation.example: A 70% recommendation means most of the signal-confidence leans one way — GRQ still makes the actual call.

dossier.def: A deep research write-up the agent files on one stock: the business, recent news, signals, bull and bear case, and a verdict.
dossier.example: Before GRQ can buy a name, it files a dossier — business, catalysts, the bear case, a verdict — so the trade has receipts.

soak.def: The trial run: the fund must trade clean for 4+ weeks (2 of them on real broker paper) before a single real dollar is at risk.
soak.example: Four clean weeks (two on IBKR paper) with no blown guardrails before real money — the soak is GRQ proving itself first.

contributions.def: Every dollar Cam and Graham have put into the fund. Total P&L and the benchmark are both measured against this — it's the money that had to be beaten.
contributions.example: Put in $25,000 total and that's the bar both Total P&L and the XIC benchmark are measured against.

fee-budget.def: A hard monthly ceiling on commissions. The order gate rejects any trade that would push this month's fees over the line — fees quietly kill small accounts.
fee-budget.example: Hit the month's commission ceiling and the gate blocks the next trade until next month — fees can't snowball.

market-value.def: What a holding is worth right now: shares held × the latest price. Add them all up, plus cash, and you get NAV.
market-value.example: 100 shares at $30 = $3,000 of market value; sum every holding plus cash and you have NAV.

unrealized-pnl.def: Paper profit or loss on a holding you still own — what you'd lock in if you sold at the current price. It isn't real until you sell.
unrealized-pnl.example: Up $400 on a stock you still hold is unrealized — a paper gain that vanishes if the price falls before you sell.

weight.def: How much of the fund one position is, as a share of NAV. The risk dial caps it so no single name can sink the whole boat.
weight.example: A $5,000 position in a $25,000 fund is a 20% weight — the risk dial caps how big any one name can get.

position.def: A holding: the shares of one stock the fund currently owns, with an average cost and a current value.
position.example: 50 shares of XIC at an average cost of $56 is a position — shares, a cost base, and a live value.

market-cap.def: A company's total stock-market value: share price × shares outstanding. Roughly what it would cost to buy the whole company.
market-cap.example: A $40 stock with 50 million shares out has a $2-billion market cap — a small-cap.

free-cash-flow.def: The cash a business actually generates after running costs and reinvestment — money it's free to return to owners or stockpile. Harder to fake than reported earnings.
free-cash-flow.example: A company can report a paper profit yet burn cash — negative free cash flow is the tell.

dividend-yield.def: The annual dividend as a percent of the share price. A $2 dividend on a $50 stock yields 4%.
dividend-yield.example: That same $2 dividend yields 5% if the stock falls to $40 — a high yield can flag a falling price.

short-interest.def: The share of a stock that traders have borrowed and sold, betting it falls. High short interest signals bearishness — and can fuel a sharp 'short squeeze' if the price rises instead.
short-interest.example: 20% of the float sold short, then good news hits — shorts scramble to buy back and the price rockets.

dilution.def: When a company issues new shares, each existing share owns a smaller slice. Common with cash-hungry small-caps — it can quietly erode your stake even as the business grows.
dilution.example: A cash-strapped miner doubles its share count to raise money — your slice of the company just halved.

stop-loss.def: A pre-set exit: if a holding falls to this price, the agent sells to cap the damage. The level is set by the risk dial (e.g. −8% on Balanced).
stop-loss.example: Buy at $20 with an −8% stop and the agent auto-sells near $18.40 if it rolls over.

take-profit.def: The mirror of a stop: a pre-set level where the agent banks a winner so a paper gain doesn't evaporate. Also set by the risk dial.
take-profit.example: A +20% take-profit on that $20 entry banks the win near $24 instead of round-tripping it.

expected-return.def: The upside the agent's price target implies from today's price — a hypothesis with a horizon, not a promise. The track record builds as targets resolve.
expected-return.example: A $30 target on a $24 stock is a +25% expected return — if the thesis plays out.

price-target.def: Where the agent thinks a stock could trade — a near-term swing target and a 12-month view. The basis for expected return, judged honestly when it plays out.
price-target.example: GRQ might post a near-term target of $26 and a 12-month target of $34 on the same name.

commission.def: The broker's fee per trade. Small but relentless: GRQ won't take a trade unless it's worth at least 3× the round-trip commissions.
commission.example: At ~$5 a trade, churning a $200 position to scalp 2% loses money to fees — exactly what the 3× rule blocks.

moat.def: A durable advantage that protects a company's profits from competitors — brand, network effects, low costs, switching costs. Wide moats compound for years.
moat.example: Switching your whole company off one software suite is painful — that friction is the vendor's moat.

pe.def: Share price divided by annual earnings per share — how many years of current profit you're paying for. High P/E = the market expects growth; low = skepticism or value.
pe.example: A $50 stock earning $2.50 a share trades at a P/E of 20 — twenty years of today's profit.

eps.def: A company's profit divided by its shares — the per-share slice of what it earned that quarter. Analysts publish an estimate beforehand; the reported actual beating or missing it is what usually moves the stock.
eps.example: Estimate $1.20, reports $1.35 → a beat. The market often cares more about the beat/miss than the raw number.

earnings.def: A company's quarterly scorecard — revenue, profit, and EPS for the last three months, plus its outlook. Filed before the open (BMO) or after the close (AMC), it's the single biggest scheduled event for a stock.
earnings.example: MU and AMD both reported after the close — the reaction shows up in the next session's price.

etf.def: A basket of stocks bought as one ticker. XIC, for instance, holds the whole TSX — instant diversification in a single trade.
etf.example: One share of XIC gives you a slice of every big Canadian company at once.

swing-trade.def: Holding for days to a few weeks to catch a price 'swing' — longer than day-trading, shorter than buy-and-hold. GRQ's core style.
swing-trade.example: Buy a breakout, aim to sell into strength two or three weeks later — a swing, not a day-trade or a forever-hold.

confidence.def: How sure the agent (or a signal) is about a call, 0–100. A self-assessment, not a probability — and the agent needs ≥75% conviction before the gate will let it buy.
confidence.example: The agent can like a name at 60%, but the gate won't let it buy until conviction clears 75%.

confidence-levers.def: The specific, falsifiable things that would reframe Alfred's call — what's pinning the confidence below 100. Each is either a gap we could close (info that exists but we don't have — read the latest filing, no guidance feed) or a catalyst still to land (an event on a known date — earnings, a ruling). It says which way resolving it would move the call, how much, and how we'd learn it.
confidence-levers.example: A name might be a Hold only because earnings are two weeks out and would confirm or kill the margin thesis — once they land, the call gets re-rated.

the-tape.def: The fund's value through the trading day, open to now — the intraday line of NAV. (Old trading-floor slang: the ticker 'tape' that printed live prices.)
the-tape.example: If the Tape is down 1.2% at noon, the fund's NAV has slipped 1.2% since this morning's open.

agent-call.def: GRQ's own judgment on a name — buy, accumulate, hold, watch, trim, avoid, or sell — weighing the business, the news, and the price. Distinct from the signal consensus (a technicals formula); when the two disagree, the 'why' below explains it.
agent-call.example: GRQ can rate a name 'accumulate' even while the technical signal reads neutral — the 'why' explains the gap.

universe.def: The list of stocks the agent is allowed to buy. A name joins by being promoted — any member (or the agent itself, under code-enforced rules) can promote a researched candidate once it clears an automated liquidity screen. Only then can the agent buy it, and every order still clears the order gate.
universe.example: A name has to clear the liquidity screen to enter the universe — only then can the agent buy it; until then it's a candidate.

watchlist.def: The names you're watching — your personal interest list. Each member's watches stack up as faces on a name, and the agent researches every watched name (a dossier, signals, its call). Watching is separate from the universe: a name stays on your watchlist even after it's promoted, and the agent still can't trade it until it's in the universe.
watchlist.example: Cam and Graham can both watch the same name — you'll see both faces — and GRQ researches it; it can't trade it until it's promoted into the universe.

analyst-target.def: The average 12-month price target from the Wall Street analysts who cover the stock. A useful outside check on Alfred's call — when GRQ and the street sharply disagree, it's worth asking who's right.
analyst-target.example: If the street's average target is $40 and GRQ's is $28, someone's wrong — worth knowing why before you buy.

capital-gains.def: Tax on the profit when you sell for more than you paid. In Canada (non-registered accounts), half the gain is taxable at your marginal rate — so a 10% gain is worth less after tax. Inside a TFSA, gains are tax-free.
capital-gains.example: Sell for a $1,000 gain in a non-registered account and ~$500 is taxable at your rate; in a TFSA the whole $1,000 is yours.

tfsa.def: A registered account where investment gains are tax-free. The catch: trade too actively and the CRA can reclassify it as a business and tax everything — so a swing-trade cadence (not day-trading) matters.
tfsa.example: Day-trade inside a TFSA and the CRA can call it a business and tax it all — a swing cadence keeps it tax-free.

rrsp.def: A registered account: contributions reduce this year's taxable income and growth is tax-deferred — you pay tax as income when you withdraw in retirement.
rrsp.example: A $5,000 RRSP contribution lowers this year's taxable income; you pay tax later, as income, when you draw it down.

13f.def: A quarterly report big investment managers (over $100M) must file listing their U.S. stock holdings. It's a snapshot, filed up to ~45 days after quarter-end, and it shows only longs and options — never short positions.
13f.example: Buffett's Q1 13F landing in mid-May shows what Berkshire held back in March — useful colour, stale for timing.

qoq.def: The change from one quarter (a three-month reporting period) to the next. Here, '+24 QoQ' means 24 more institutions hold the stock than in the previous quarter's 13F filings — a measure of whether big money is building or trimming the position.
qoq.example: '+24 QoQ' means 24 more institutions hold the name than last quarter — big money building the position.

form-4.def: The filing a company's executives, directors, and 10%+ owners must submit within two days of trading its stock. Open-market purchases are the meaningful 'insider buying' signal; option exercises and grants are noise.
form-4.example: A CEO buying $250k of her own stock on the open market files a Form 4 — that's the buy worth noticing.

insider.def: A company's own officers, directors, or 10%+ owners. Their trades are disclosed on Form 4 — when they buy on the open market with their own money, it's often read as confidence in the business.
insider.example: When three insiders buy with their own cash the same week, it's often read as real confidence in the business.

put-option.def: A bet that a stock falls — it gains value as the price drops. In a 13F a put shows up as a 'holding', but it's a bearish position, not ownership of the shares.
put-option.example: A put line in a 13F isn't ownership — it's a bet the stock falls, so don't read it as a vote of confidence.

call-option.def: A leveraged bet that a stock rises — it gains value as the price climbs. A call line in a 13F is a bullish add-on, not plain share ownership.
call-option.example: A fund adding calls on a name is leaning bullish with leverage — a louder version of buying the shares.

cluster-buying.def: Several different insiders at one company buying its stock around the same time — a stronger signal than any single purchase, since it's harder to dismiss as one person's hunch.
cluster-buying.example: One director buying is a shrug; five insiders buying the same week is a cluster — much harder to dismiss.

congress-trade.def: Members of Congress must disclose their stock trades — but only as dollar ranges (e.g. $1M–$5M) and up to ~45 days late. Colour on what well-connected people are doing, not a holdings list and not a timing signal.
congress-trade.example: A disclosure might read '$1M–$5M, filed 40 days late' — colour on the well-connected, not a holdings list or a timing signal.

llm.def: An AI trained on vast amounts of text to read, reason, and write. GRQ's agent is an LLM; The Race pits several different ones against the same market data.
llm.example: Ask one 'should we buy XIC today?' and it works through the fund's data like an analyst would.

the-race.def: Each session the same data is handed to several AI models. Only Opus (the 'champion') actually trades; the rest are 'shadow' challengers that just say what they'd do — so we can score who's right without risking a dollar.
the-race.example: At a 1pm check-in Opus buys SHOP while Grok would've held — both calls get logged and marked to the live price.

opus.def: Anthropic's most capable model, and the ONLY one in The Race that places real trades. Every other model is shadow-only.
opus.example: When GRQ actually buys something, it was Opus's call that cleared the gate.

sonnet.def: Anthropic's faster, lighter Claude. A shadow challenger in The Race — it proposes, never trades — and runs free on the fund's existing Claude plan.
sonnet.example: Sonnet might back Opus's buy, or argue it'd wait for a cleaner entry.

haiku.def: Anthropic's smallest, quickest Claude. GRQ uses it for cheap triage — deciding whether a news event is even worth a full analysis — not for trade decisions.
haiku.example: A routine headline? Haiku says 'ignore' so the expensive model never has to wake up.

gpt.def: OpenAI's flagship model, racing shadow-only. A different lineage from Claude, so it's a genuinely independent second opinion.
gpt.example: Reading the same data, GPT-5.1 might rank a different name as the day's best setup.

gemini.def: Google's flagship model, racing shadow-only. It 'reasons' visibly before answering — thorough, but the priciest challenger to run.
gemini.example: Gemini may spend a paragraph weighing both sides before settling on HOLD.

glm.def: An open-weight model from Chinese lab Z.ai (Zhipu). A shadow challenger — strong reasoning at a fraction of the frontier price.
glm.example: GLM-4.6 costs a fraction of the frontier models per call yet still makes a credible call.

deepseek.def: An open-weight model from Chinese lab DeepSeek, known for near-frontier quality at a tiny price. The cheapest challenger in The Race.
deepseek.example: DeepSeek weighs in on every session for cents a day.

grok.def: The model from Elon Musk's xAI, and a shadow challenger — it rounds out the field so all four major frontier labs are represented.
grok.example: Grok 4.3 gets the exact same prompt as Opus and logs what it would have done.

llama.def: Meta's open-weight model and the most widely self-run open model in the West. A shadow challenger — a different lineage again from the frontier labs and the Chinese open-weights.
llama.example: Reading the same data as Opus, Llama logs the call it would have made.

options-positioning.def: What the options market reveals about how big traders are betting on a stock. GRQ never trades options — it reads this only as a signal about the underlying stock (where the crowd and the dealers are leaning).
options-positioning.example: Heavy put buying + dealers positioned to amplify moves can flag a name the market is bracing on.

gamma-exposure.def: Market-makers who sold the options must constantly buy/sell the stock to stay hedged. When net gamma is POSITIVE they trade AGAINST moves → the stock gets 'pinned' / range-bound. When NEGATIVE they trade WITH moves → swings get amplified and trendy.
gamma-exposure.example: Negative gamma into a selloff means dealers keep selling as it drops — the move feeds on itself.

put-call-ratio.def: Puts divided by calls (by open interest or today's volume). Above 1 = more puts → defensive / bearish lean or hedging; below 1 = call-heavy → bullish or speculative. A crowd-positioning gauge, best read as a contrarian extreme.
put-call-ratio.example: A put/call of 1.9 on the day means heavy defensive put flow.

implied-volatility.def: The size of move the options market is PRICING IN over the next ~month, as an annualized %. High IV = the market expects big swings (fear or a catalyst); low IV = calm expected. It's the market's forecast, not a fact.
implied-volatility.example: 50% IV on a stock means options are priced for a much wilder ride than one at 20%.

call-wall.def: The strike prices where dealer hedging is heaviest. The call wall often acts like a ceiling/magnet (resistance); the put wall like a floor (support). Not guarantees — just where options-driven hedging concentrates.
call-wall.example: A call wall at $400 can cap a rally as dealers sell into it to stay hedged.

volatility-skew.def: How much more the market pays for downside protection (out-of-the-money puts) than upside (calls), in basis points. A high positive skew = the market is bidding up crash insurance → fear; flat/low skew = complacency.
volatility-skew.example: A 200bp skew means puts are notably 'fearful' versus calls — the market's paying up for protection.

social-buzz.def: GRQ's own loudness score for a name on retail forums — how much it's being talked about (Reddit mention volume) and whether that's accelerating. High buzz isn't a buy signal; on a name we hold it's a CROWDING/risk flag (euphoria can reverse hard). A signal we weigh, never a trade.
social-buzz.example: A holding spiking to buzz 90 means the crowd has piled in — watch for a blow-off, not a green light.

mention-velocity.def: Today's Reddit mentions for a name divided by its own trailing 7-day average. Above 1 = chatter is heating up; below 1 = cooling off. We measure it against the name's OWN history so a normally-quiet stock suddenly lighting up stands out.
mention-velocity.example: 2.0× means twice the usual daily chatter — something just grabbed retail's attention.

social-sentiment.def: The share of retail posts tagged bullish vs bearish (from Stocktwits, where users self-label each message). Noisy and easily gamed — GRQ reads it as crowd mood, not truth, and it earns trust slowly like any source. The fund never trades on it alone.
social-sentiment.example: 85% bullish on a name the crowd already owns can mean the easy money's been made.

strike.def: The fixed price written into an option contract. A call only pays off when the stock is ABOVE its strike; a put only when it's BELOW. It's the line in the sand the whole bet is measured against.
strike.example: A $105 call on a $100 stock needs the price above $105 by expiry to have any value left.

premium.def: The price you pay (to buy) or receive (to sell) for an option, quoted per share — so a $2.50 premium costs $250 for one 100-share contract. When you BUY an option, the premium is the most you can lose.
premium.example: Buy one call at a $2.50 premium and you've paid $250 and risked exactly that.

intrinsic-value.def: The part of an option's premium that is real, exercise-it-right-now value: how far in-the-money it is. A $105 call with the stock at $112 has $7 of intrinsic value. Out of the money, intrinsic value is zero.
intrinsic-value.example: Stock at $112, a $105 call: $7 is intrinsic; anything above $7 in the premium is time value.

extrinsic-value.def: The rest of the premium beyond intrinsic value — what you pay for the time and uncertainty left before expiry. It melts toward zero as expiry nears (time decay) and shrinks when implied volatility falls.
extrinsic-value.example: An at-the-money option is ALL time value — there's no intrinsic value to fall back on.

moneyness.def: Where the stock sits versus the strike. In-the-money (ITM) = the option has intrinsic value; at-the-money (ATM) = stock ≈ strike; out-of-the-money (OTM) = no intrinsic value yet, all hope and time value.
moneyness.example: Stock $100: a $90 call is ITM, a $100 call is ATM, a $110 call is OTM.

break-even.def: The stock price at which a trade's profit is exactly zero at expiry — below/above it you lose, beyond it you win. For a long call it's the strike plus the premium you paid.
break-even.example: A $105 call bought for $2.50 breaks even at $107.50 at expiry.

max-loss.def: The worst case for a position. For an option you BUY it's just the premium — defined risk. For strategies that SELL options the loss can be much larger, which is exactly why the fund only ever buys.
max-loss.example: Long a call for $250, your max loss is $250 no matter how far the stock falls.

payoff-diagram.def: The picture of a trade's profit or loss across every possible stock price. The flat parts, the kinks at the strikes, and where the line crosses zero (break-even) tell you the whole risk-and-reward shape at a glance.
payoff-diagram.example: A long call's payoff is a flat loss up to the strike, then a 45° line climbing into profit.

time-decay.def: Options lose a little value every day just from time passing, because there's less chance left for a big move. The bleed accelerates as expiry approaches. You can be right on direction and still lose if the move is too slow.
time-decay.example: Hold an at-the-money option over a quiet week and it's worth less Friday than Monday, stock unchanged.

delta.def: How much an option's premium moves per $1 move in the stock — and a rough gauge of the odds it finishes in-the-money. A 0.50 delta call gains ~50¢ for a $1 rise; deep-in-the-money options approach 1.00.
delta.example: A 0.30-delta call is ~30% likely to expire ITM and moves ~30¢ per $1 of stock.

gamma.def: How fast delta itself changes as the stock moves — the option's acceleration. Highest for at-the-money options near expiry, which is what makes those swing so violently.
gamma.example: High gamma means a small stock move can flip a near-the-money option from sleepy to fast-moving.

theta.def: The dollar amount an option loses per day from time decay, all else equal. It's negative for anything you buy — the daily rent you pay for holding the bet.
theta.example: A theta of −$5 means the position bleeds about $5 a day if nothing else changes.

vega.def: How much an option's premium changes when implied volatility moves one percentage point. Buyers are long vega — they profit if the market starts pricing in bigger swings, and lose if it calms down.
vega.example: Vega of $8 means +1 point of IV adds about $8 to the position's value.

greeks.def: The handful of sensitivities that describe how an option's price reacts: delta (to the stock), gamma (to delta itself), theta (to time), and vega (to volatility). Together they're the dashboard for any option position.
greeks.example: Reading the Greeks tells you what your position will do before the stock even moves.

expiry.def: The date an option contract dies. At expiry it's worth only its intrinsic value — anything in-the-money settles for that, anything out-of-the-money expires worthless. The deadline your thesis is racing against.
expiry.example: An OTM call still OTM at expiry simply vanishes — premium gone, lesson learned.

covered-call.def: Owning 100 shares and selling a call against them to collect premium as income. The catch: if the stock rallies past the strike your shares get called away, so you cap your upside in exchange for the cash now.
covered-call.example: Own 100 shares at $100, sell a $110 call for $2: you pocket $200 but give up gains above $110.

cash-secured-put.def: Selling a put while holding enough cash to buy the shares if assigned. You collect premium up front; if the stock falls below the strike you buy it (cushioned by the premium), otherwise you keep the premium free.
cash-secured-put.example: Sell a $95 put on a $100 stock for $2: you're paid $200 to maybe buy it at $95.

short-selling.def: Borrowing shares, selling them now, and buying them back later — a bet a stock FALLS. You profit if the price drops below where you sold, and lose if it rises. It's the trade the long-only fund can't make, and the only one whose loss has no cap.
short-selling.example: Short 100 shares at $50; if it drops to $40 you buy back for a $1,000 gain — if it runs to $80 you're down $3,000 and counting.

cost-to-borrow.def: The annualized fee you pay to borrow the shares you short — small for liquid names, brutal for hard-to-borrow ones. You also pay any dividend the stock issues while you're short. Carry that bleeds you the longer you hold.
cost-to-borrow.example: A 20%/yr borrow on a $10,000 short costs about $5.50 a day just to keep the position on.

margin-call.def: Shorting runs on borrowed collateral. If the stock rises against you and your equity falls below the broker's maintenance requirement, you're force-covered — bought back at the worst possible moment, locking in the loss. This is how shorts blow up.
margin-call.example: A short that doubles can erase your collateral and trigger a forced buy-in before you ever choose to exit.

short-squeeze.def: When a heavily-shorted stock rallies, shorts rush to buy back and cover — and that buying pushes the price up further, forcing more covering. A self-feeding spike with no long-side equivalent, and the nightmare scenario for a short.
short-squeeze.example: A crowded short doubling in days as everyone scrambles to cover at once.

day-trading.def: Buying and selling the same stock within a single day — often held minutes to hours — to profit from small intraday moves, never holding overnight. The opposite of GRQ's buy-and-hold-on-conviction style, and it's a hard §6 limit for the fund (no same-day round trips).
day-trading.example: Buy at 10am, sell at noon, buy again at 2pm — all in one name, all in one day.

bid-ask-spread.def: The gap between the highest price buyers will pay (the bid) and the lowest sellers will take (the ask). You buy at the ask and sell at the bid, so every round trip starts underwater by the spread — a hidden cost that adds up fast when you trade often.
bid-ask-spread.example: Bid $99.90 / ask $100.10: buy and immediately sell and you're already down 20¢ a share.

slippage.def: The difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got — because the market moved or your order was big enough to push it. Together with commissions and the spread, it's what quietly eats a day-trader's thin per-trade margins.
slippage.example: You aim to buy at $100 but the fill comes back at $100.08 — that 8¢ is slippage.

pattern-day-trader.def: A US rule: make 4+ day trades in 5 business days in a margin account under $25,000 and you're flagged as a Pattern Day Trader and restricted from further day trading until you top up. Cash accounts avoid it but hit settlement limits instead.
pattern-day-trader.example: A $10k margin account gets locked from day trading after its fourth round trip in a week.

settlement.def: Stock trades take a day or two to officially settle (cash and shares change hands). In a cash account you can't rebuy with proceeds that haven't settled yet — doing so is a 'good-faith violation' — which caps how fast you can churn without margin.
settlement.example: Sell today, and that cash isn't fully available to redeploy until it settles a day later.

days-to-cover.def: Short interest divided by average daily volume — roughly how many days of normal trading it would take every short to buy back. A high number means shorts are packed into a small exit, which makes a squeeze more violent.
days-to-cover.example: Days-to-cover of 8 means it'd take over a week of average volume for shorts to all cover.

long-call.def: Buying a call outright — the simplest bullish option bet. Leveraged upside if the stock rises past the strike; the premium you paid is the most you can lose.
long-call.example: Buy one $105 call for $2.50 and your worst case is −$250, no matter how hard the stock falls.

ticker.def: The short code a stock trades under on a specific exchange — SHOP, XIC, AAPL. It's an address, not a name: the same letters can point at completely different companies on different exchanges.
ticker.example: SPCX on the TSX is a Canadian certificate tracking SpaceX — not a SpaceX share; always check where a ticker lives.

ipo.def: The day a private company first sells shares to the public. It's the one time buying the stock hands money to the company itself — every trade after that is just investors swapping shares between themselves.
ipo.example: Buy at the IPO and you're funding the company; buy the next morning and you're paying whoever got in first.

index.def: A formula-weighted basket of stocks used as a market thermometer — the S&P 500, the TSX Composite. Most are cap-weighted, so the biggest companies dominate the reading.
index.example: 'The market rose 1%' means an index did — which mostly means its ten biggest names did.

market-order.def: 'Fill me now, at whatever the market's asking.' You're guaranteed the fill, not the price — it crosses the spread and takes whatever's on the other side, which in a thin name can surprise you.
market-order.example: A market buy in an illiquid stock can fill several levels up the book — you asked for now, not for cheap.

limit-order.def: 'Fill me at this price or better — or not at all.' You're guaranteed the price, not the fill; the market is under no obligation to come to you.
limit-order.example: A $98 limit bid on a $100 stock only fills if the price comes down to meet it — plenty of limits expire lonely.

market-maker.def: A firm that quotes both a bid and an ask all day, in thousands of names, earning the spread over and over — in exchange for making sure there's always someone to trade with.
market-maker.example: Your 10:47am buy probably didn't find a human seller — a market maker took the other side and moved on.

liquidity.def: How much of a stock you can buy or sell without moving the price against yourself. Liquid names have tight spreads and deep volume; illiquid ones punish you on the way in AND the way out.
liquidity.example: GRQ's liquidity screen blocks names that trade too thin — a position you can't exit cleanly is a trap with a ticker.

volume.def: How many shares changed hands in a period. A price move on heavy volume has real conviction behind it; the same move on thin volume is a shrug that can reverse by lunch.
volume.example: A 5% pop on 10× average volume means money changed its mind; on a trickle, it means almost nothing.

dividend.def: A cash payout per share from the company's profits, usually quarterly. On the ex-dividend date the price drops by roughly the payout — it's your own money arriving, not a bonus.
dividend.example: A $1 dividend lands and the stock opens about $1 lower — buying the day before to 'grab it' achieves nothing.

stock-split.def: Cutting the pizza into more slices: a 2-for-1 split doubles your share count and halves the price. You own exactly what you owned before — splits are psychology and convenience, not value.
stock-split.example: An $800 stock splits 4-for-1 to trade at $200 — nothing about the business changed.

buyback.def: A company buying back and cancelling its own shares — dilution in reverse. Fewer shares exist, so each remaining one owns a bigger slice of the business. Only value-adding if the shares were bought cheap.
buyback.example: Retire 10% of the share count and every holder's slice grows ~11% — no cheque mailed, same effect over time.

total-return.def: Price change PLUS dividends (ideally reinvested). The honest way to compare investments — judging a dividend payer on price alone shortchanges it.
total-return.example: A stock flat on price that paid 4% in dividends beat one that rose 3% and paid nothing.

mer.def: The yearly fee a fund quietly deducts from its own value, in percent. Tiny for plain index ETFs, up to ~2% for active funds — and it compounds against you every single year.
mer.example: XIC charges about 0.06%; a 2% mutual fund costs 33× more for the privilege of probably trailing it.

cdr.def: A TSX-listed, CAD-hedged certificate representing a fraction of a big (usually US) company's share. It tracks the company without being the actual share — and the built-in FX hedge changes how it behaves.
cdr.example: SPCX.TO is a ~$36 CAD-hedged SpaceX CDR — a way to hold the story in loonies, not the Nasdaq share itself.

currency-risk.def: Hold a US stock from Canada and you're making two bets: the stock, and the exchange rate. A move in the US dollar changes your CAD-measured return even when the stock stands still.
currency-risk.example: A US name gains 5% while the USD slips 5% against the loonie — in CAD, your gain just evaporated.

guidance.def: Management's own forecast for the coming quarter or year, issued alongside earnings. It often moves the stock more than the reported numbers — the market prices the future, and guidance IS the future, straight from the people running the place.
guidance.example: A company beats the quarter but cuts full-year guidance — the stock falls anyway.

leverage.def: Investing with borrowed money, so gains AND losses are amplified. 2× leverage turns a −25% dip into −50% of your capital — and a margin call can force you out before any recovery arrives. GRQ's fund is barred from it.
leverage.example: Put up $10k, borrow $10k, buy $20k of stock: a 25% market dip just cost you half your money.

correlation.def: How much two holdings move together. Diversification only works when correlations are low — holdings that fail for different reasons. The catch: in a real panic, correlations rush toward 1 and everything falls at once.
correlation.example: Ten Canadian banks isn't diversification — it's one bet, held ten times.

compounding.def: Growth earning growth on itself — the engine of long-term investing. Rule of 72: divide 72 by your annual return to get the years to double. Small rate differences become enormous outcome differences over decades.
compounding.example: $10,000 at 7% is ~$20k in a decade and ~$80k in three — the last doubling earns more than the first two combined.
